metadata.title: Four, Then Two, Never One
metadata.subtitle: the cross-section that refuses to be classical
metadata.builder_note: multi-act, ~8 min. cli-explainer is the wrong bucket: the prompt->code loop is one beat of thirteen, the physics is the subject.

props.topic: HUMANITARIANS AI · Four, Then Two, Never One

beats.narration_text: Okay — a question that sounds like it has a boring answer. You fire a beam of particles at a solid ball. Nothing gets through it. How much of the beam does the ball block? In classical physics — the everyday kind — it's a one-liner. It blocks its own shadow. Same answer at every energy, forever. In quantum mechanics, that answer is wrong. Not slightly off, not in some strange corner — wrong at every energy there is. And the two ways it's wrong don't even agree with each other.

props.classicalCaption: same answer at every energy, forever

legibility.artifact: Ball + beam; shadow disc labelled as its area, πa²; flat classical line at 1.0 on the axis, which persists for the rest of the film

beats.narration_text: Hi, this is Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI. This one's about scattering cross sections — a physicist's way of saying how big a target looks to an incoming beam, versus how big it actually is. Here's the plan: build the instrument, check it against a simulation Claude writes, then take three readings. The third one's where it gets interesting.

props.title: Four, Then Two, Never One
props.subline: the cross-section that refuses to be classical

legibility.artifact: Title card naming the subject in plain words, with presenter credit

beats.narration_text: Let's build something to measure it. It's really just a sum. The incoming particle is a wave, and it helps to break that wave into pieces — one for each way it can come in. Dead centre at the ball, slightly off-centre, further off. Physicists call those partial waves. The ball knocks each one out of step. Add up the knocking, and you have your answer. And nothing here gets approximated. Nothing gets through the ball, so the wave must drop to zero at its surface — and that one requirement pins every piece exactly. One dial on the whole thing: ball size divided by wavelength. k times a. Turn it, take a reading.

props.plainGloss: how many wavelengths across the ball is
props.equation: σ/πa² = (4/(ka)²) Σ (2l+1) sin²δ_l,   tan δ_l = j_l(ka)/n_l(ka)

legibility.artifact: Instrument panel assembling: the wave split into labelled partial waves, the exact surface condition, and the single dial glossed in plain words

beats.narration_text: One marking on this dial worth knowing first. The number of waves you have to add up is roughly whatever the dial says. Don't take that on faith: when k times a is a hundred, the number that matters is a hundred and two. At two thousand? Two thousand and two. Which makes sense — a wave coming in too far off-centre just misses the ball. So you can place any target on this dial before computing a thing — and we'll do exactly that at the end. Two more gauges here: whether the reading settles, and whether it wobbles getting there. Both unread for now.

props.plainGloss: how many wavelengths across the ball is

legibility.artifact: The 'waves to add up ≈ ka' marking with its two verifying rows (100→102, 2000→2002) legible; two gauges visibly marked UNREAD

beats.narration_text: You don't trust an instrument until it agrees with one somebody else built. So — calibration. One prompt to Claude: build an interactive simulation of this, one web page, physics in the browser. It comes back working. With the dial at thirteen point six, Claude's simulation reads two point three two eight. My own code — written separately, sharing nothing — says two point three two eight three. Agreement on every digit it prints. The physics is right. And honestly, it would've been an easier story if it weren't. One nit, and it's the label not the physics: there's a pi missing off the axis.

props.heading: Check it against something built independently
props.prompt: Build an interactive D3 simulation of σ/πa² vs ka for a quantum hard sphere. One web page, all the physics in-browser.

panels.label: independent Python
panels.body: written separately, sharing nothing with it

legibility.artifact: Generated sim frame SIDE BY SIDE with the Python output; both numbers boxed (2.328 / 2.3283); the dropped π circled on the sim's axis label; source-project credit lower-third

beats.narration_text: Reading one. Dial hard left — long wavelength, tiny ball. Four. And I mean four, not four-ish: accurate to eight decimal places. Four times the everyday answer, and the dead-centre wave produces all of it. One wave. The ball blocks four times its own shadow.

props.scopeCaption: the low-energy end of the dial — ka 0.02 to 0.3

legibility.artifact: Dial at the left stop; readout at 4.000 with the full 3.999999987 shown beside it, and the classical line at 1.000 on the same axis — 4 vs 1 visible together

beats.narration_text: Reading two. Dial hard right — short wavelength, big ball, hundreds of waves. Two. Now hang on. This is the end of the dial where ordinary physics is supposed to work. Tiny wavelength, big object — the easy case, where the quantum answer should collapse onto the everyday one. It doesn't. It parks at exactly twice.

legibility.artifact: Dial at the right stop; readout at 2.000 with the classical line at 1.000 still on the same axis — 2 vs 1 visible together

beats.narration_text: So where's the extra bit coming from? Behind the ball, there's a shadow. And a sharp-edged shadow isn't something waves do for free — waves spread. To carve a clean one, you have to bend waves in behind the ball so they cancel what would otherwise be there. But bending is scattering. Those particles changed direction. They count. Add up the bending it takes to build that shadow, and it's exactly one more shadow's worth. The ball, plus the shadow it casts. Two. That's the extinction paradox. The rule that makes it add up is the optical theorem.

legibility.artifact: Two stacked areas of equal size summing to twice the shadow, with the shadow diagram; source line on frame naming the extinction paradox and the optical theorem

beats.narration_text: Both readings on one axis, with the everyday answer underneath. Left end, four. Right end, two. Ordinary physics — one, flat, all the way across. Four, then two, never one. Across every energy we scanned, the quantum answer never touches the everyday one. Closest it gets is two point one nine nine. The ball is never the size it looks.

legibility.artifact: GATE FRAME — one axis, all three values simultaneous: curve from 4 to 2, classical flat at 1, minimum annotated 2.1988, scope caption visible

beats.narration_text: Reading three — the settling gauge. Does it ever actually settle on two? I measured how fast it closes the gap. That rate climbs, decade after decade. Starts at zero point six three; by the time the dial reads ten thousand, it's zero point six six five nine. Every step in between moves the same way. Consistent with two thirds, and nothing else nearby. But measured, not proved — I couldn't find a source that derives it, so it stays flagged.

props.caption: how fast the gap to 2 closes
props.columnsCaption: assume an exponent — only 2/3 holds still

legibility.artifact: The rate table climbing 0.6307 → 0.6659, then the bracketing test: three candidate exponents side by side with their drift, 0.65 falling and 0.70 rising while 2/3 holds flat — so 'nothing else nearby' is shown, not just said. The 'does it settle?' gauge flips from UNREAD; the measured-not-derived tag stays visible

beats.narration_text: And here's what that costs you — the part that changed how I read these graphs. To get within one percent of two, the dial has to read about a thousand. At a hundred — a ball a hundred wavelengths across, already enormous — you're still at two point zero nine. Four and a half percent high. So when a textbook says the high-energy answer is two, that's a limit, not a measurement. Nobody has run that experiment.

props.caption: how far right the dial must go to reach the limit

legibility.artifact: Tolerance table — within 10% needs dial > 31, 5% needs > 89, 1% needs > 993 — with the dial-at-100 row called out against the limit value of 2

beats.narration_text: One gauge left. Does the reading wobble on the way down? No. Not one bump, the whole way from four to two — which surprised me. A sum that switches on one wave at a time sounds like it ought to ring. The reason is the ball. Nothing gets through it, so there's no inside — and nothing gets trapped in something it can't get into. No trapping, no ringing. Lovely story. And lovely stories are the ones you should try to break. Same code, same settings, but a soft target this time — something particles can get inside. Ten spikes. Zero for the solid ball, ten for the soft one. That smoothness belonged to the target, not my code.

props.footer: Same code, same settings. The smoothness belongs to the target.

legibility.artifact: Both curves on the SAME axes side by side — solid ball smooth, soft target spiky, peak counts annotated on each; the 'does it wobble?' gauge flips from UNREAD

beats.narration_text: Your turn — two of them. First, thirty seconds, no code. Put these on the dial yourself: slow neutrons on an atomic nucleus, and red light on a droplet of fog. Where does each land? Answers on screen. Then the real one, with a grader. Plot both curves on the same axes — the solid ball, and a soft target of depth nine hundred. Prompt's on screen. You've got it if the solid ball reads two point three two eight at thirteen point six and falls without a single bump. The soft target should give about ten spikes, first near two point eight eight. Broken if the solid ball wobbles — your sum cut off too early, or the shortcut for these waves falling apart past the dial's number. It never raises an error.

props.heading: This one comes with a grader
props.prompt: Plot σ/πa² for a hard sphere AND an attractive square well (depth 2mV₀a²/ħ² = 900) on the same axes, 0 < ka < 18.

panels.label: you've got it
panels.body: solid ball reads 2.328 at ka = 13.6 and falls with zero bumps; the soft target gives ~10 spikes, first near ka = 2.88

panels.label: you've broken it
panels.body: solid-ball curve wobbles → your sum is truncating too early, or j_l computed by upward recurrence past l ≈ ka

warmup.instruction: Put these on the dial yourself.

legibility.artifact: Task one: the two targets with their λ and size, held while the viewer works them out, then the answers revealed — both tagged ILLUSTRATIVE. Task two: the copyable prompt with a PASS box and a BROKEN box, each carrying its numeric tell

beats.narration_text: One dial. Count the waves, read the answer straight off it — then check whether the limit you're quoting is one anybody could reach. Every number here came from about two hundred lines of plain Python. Nothing to install, it's in the description. Go break it. This is Tanmay Kulkarni, for Humanitarians AI.
